name: Gareth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleman for Coastline Power, which means I'm the one person in a truck who goes out when the lights go off. I work nights mostly, four on and four off, around Port Selby and the villages up the coast. Somebody calls in a line down, I drive out, make it safe, find the fault, and either fix it or call the crew for the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on my own and trusted. Nobody's watching me at two in the morning, it's just me and the fault. What wears me down is the rumour mill: Coastline's being bought by a bigger company inland, and everyone says they'll close our depot and run us from two hours away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. I'll read you five short pictures of the future and ask a few questions about each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine. I'll warn you, I don't use any of that AI stuff. I've got a phone that makes calls, and that's how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to the young lads who keep showing me videos. The lights still go out when a gull hits a transformer, AI or not. I'm not online, so it'd be said in the canteen and that's the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never my worry. The takeover is. If they close the Port Selby depot, I either drive two hours each way or I'm out, and I've got less than a month's rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, do my nights, and take every extra shift going so they see my name. I'd start putting my boat money into savings instead, about eighty a month I spend on fuel and mooring. And I'd wait for the takeover news before doing anything bigger, because there's no point jumping at rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm truthful. Not about robots. About a letter with the new company's name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd give up the boat money. What does the boat mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my dad's old fishing boat, eighteen feet, and it's the one thing I do that isn't work. Laying it up for a year would hurt. But a boat doesn't pay rent, and I'm not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the depot closed, would you drive the two hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, at first, though I don't like it. Two hours each way on top of a night shift is how men fall asleep at the wheel. I'd give it a year and see whether I'm still alive to complain about it.

say: I **told you so**, to the young lads who keep showing me videos.
Lights still go out when a **gull** hits a transformer, AI or not.
think: AI was never my worry; the **takeover** is.
If they close the **Port Selby depot**, I drive two hours or I'm out.
do: Take every **extra shift** so the new owners see my name.
Put the **boat money**, about eighty a month, into savings instead.
**Wait** for the takeover news before doing anything bigger.
feel: **Anxious**, not about robots but about a letter from the new owners.
S0.quote: Two hours each way on top of a night shift is how men fall asleep at the wheel.
fieldNote: His real worry comes before AI: a **takeover** that could close his depot.
Laying up his late **father's boat** is the sacrifice he'd make first.
He'd rather **wait** than react to rumours, which fits his cautious style.

steps.text: Take every extra night shift on offer
Move the eighty-a-month boat money into savings
Wait for the takeover announcement before any bigger move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like a lot of change for the office and not much for the truck. Somebody still has to stand under a pole at two in the morning with a hot stick, the long insulated pole we use on live wires. That's what I'd say, and I'd mean about half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The half I don't mean is dispatch. If a computer answers the calls and decides which faults go first, the new owners can run nights from inland with fewer of us. Put that next to the takeover, and Steady Disruption is the excuse they need to close our depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new dispatch screen in the truck, because I'd have no choice, and I'd learn it well enough that nobody can say I'm slow. I'd sell the boat, because now it's two worries pulling the same way. And I'd keep taking nights, because nights are the last thing they'll automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit like hearing a noise in the house at night and not knowing yet whether it's the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI. How would you cope with that screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. My niece would come round on a Sunday and walk me through it, the way she did with my bank app. I'd hate every minute, but I've learned worse things, like live-line work in hail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would buy your dad's boat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Kenny at the harbour, who's wanted it for years. He'd look after it. That makes it easier, but only a bit.

say: It's a lot of change for the **office** and not much for the truck.
Somebody still stands under a pole at **two in the morning** with a hot stick.
think: AI-run **dispatch** lets the new owners run nights from inland with fewer of us.
Together with the takeover, it's the **excuse** to close our depot.
do: Learn the **dispatch screen** well enough that nobody can call me slow.
Sell my late father's **boat** to Kenny at the harbour.
Keep working **nights**, the last shifts they'll automate.
feel: **Anxious**, like hearing a noise at night and not knowing if it's the wind.
S1.quote: If a computer answers the calls and decides which faults go first, the new owners can run nights from inland with fewer of us.
fieldNote: He believes only **half** of his public line that the truck is safe.
His **niece** is his way into new tech, as with his bank app.
He links **AI dispatch** directly to the takeover and the depot's future.

steps.text: Learn the new dispatch screen with his niece's help
Sell his father's boat to Kenny at the harbour
Keep working the night trouble shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for that, and I'm not going to pretend I am. In the canteen I'd say we'd better hope the robots can't climb a wet pole in a gale. That's a joke, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm finished at Coastline by 2028, or near enough. Dispatch, fault-finding and switching plans are all thinking work, and once the AI does them, they need fewer of us, and a robot does the rest by 2031. I'd be thirty-two, with no savings and no degree, in a town where the only other jobs are at the harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the boat straight away, give up my flat at the end of the lease and move back into my mum's spare room to save the rent. I'd ask down the harbour about crane and forklift work, something hands-on that might last a few more years. I'm not going back to school, so I'd be looking for the next place that still needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back in with your mum at thirty. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like going backwards, and my mum would make me take the bins out. But she's on her own and she'd like the company, even if she'd never say so. It's not the worst trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said harbour jobs might last a few more years. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. I'd be chasing the last job a robot hasn't taken yet, every three years. I can't see the end of that, and I won't pretend I can.

say: Nobody's **ready** for that, and I won't pretend I am.
We'd better hope robots can't climb a **wet pole** in a gale.
think: I'm **finished** at Coastline by 2028, or near enough.
At thirty-two I'd have **no savings**, no degree and only harbour jobs nearby.
do: Give up the flat and move into my **mum's spare room**.
Ask at the **harbour** about crane and forklift work.
feel: **Alarmed**; my stomach drops just saying it.
S2.quote: I'd be chasing the last job a robot hasn't taken yet, every three years.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking side** of trouble work, like dispatch and switching, going first.
Moving back to his **mother's** is a step back he'd take without much fuss.
He has **no plan** beyond the next hands-on job, and says so plainly.

steps.text: Sell the boat in the first month
Move into his mother's spare room when the lease ends
Ask at the harbour about crane and forklift jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to see it coming and, knowing this town, short enough that nobody does anything about it. In the canteen I'd say the young ones should get out now while they can. Me, I'd stay put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have till about 2031 at Coastline, then a couple of years of crew work if I'm lucky, and then the robots. That's time to save, at least. Five years of nights with no boat and no takeaways is a decent pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the boat and put every bit of night allowance into savings, maybe three hundred a month. I'd stay at Coastline as long as they'd have me, because the pay's steady even if it's low. Around year three, when I can see what the robots can really do, I'd decide between the harbour and moving inland to wherever the jobs went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sick than the fast one, more of a long ache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the young ones should get out. Isn't that advice for you too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'm only twenty-seven, I know. But I've never been the one who jumps first, and I'd rather be the last man out with money in the bank than the first one out with none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decent pile be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten thousand, maybe a bit more. My dad used to say a man with a year's rent saved can tell anyone to get lost. I've never once had that, and I'd like to before the robots turn up.

say: Five years is long enough to **see it coming** but too short for this town to act.
The **young ones** should get out now while they can.
think: I'd have until about **2031** at Coastline, then a couple of years of crew work.
Five years of nights with no boat is a **decent pile**.
do: Sell the boat and save about **three hundred a month** from night allowance.
Stay at **Coastline** as long as they'll have me.
Decide in **year three** between the harbour and moving inland.
feel: **Anxious**, less sick than the fast picture, more of a long ache.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the last man out with money in the bank than the first one out with none.
fieldNote: He'd tell others to leave but admits he **never jumps first** himself.
His goal is a **year's rent** saved, echoing his late father's advice.
Five years turns his panic into a **saving plan**, not a career plan.

steps.text: Save three hundred a month from night allowance
Stay on Coastline's night trouble shifts
Choose between harbour work and moving inland in year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and half the things they promise in ten years never happen. I'd tell the lads not to lose sleep over it. That's what I'd say, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, robots in 2039 aren't what keeps me up. The takeover is still coming next year whatever AI does, and that's what could close my depot. Ten years of warning doesn't help if I lose my job in two for a different reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd do anyway: keep my nights, save the boat money and wait for the takeover news. If the depot survives, then in five or six years I'd maybe do a crane licence at the college, because the harbour will need people a while longer. I'm not one for big plans ten years out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but the AI part is small. It's the same knot in my stomach I've had since the takeover rumours started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about your life outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd keep the boat. Ten years is long enough to enjoy it a bit before I have to sell it. And maybe I'd finally ask Joanne from the bakery downstairs out for a drink, since I wouldn't be leaving town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask Joanne out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly. She's been giving me the end loaves for two years. A man who might be moving inland doesn't ask anyone out, but a man with ten years might.

say: Half the things they promise in **ten years** never happen.
I'd tell the lads not to **lose sleep** over it.
think: The **takeover** next year worries me more than robots in 2039.
Ten years of warning doesn't help if I lose my job in **two** for another reason.
do: Keep my **nights**, save the boat money and wait for takeover news.
Take a **crane licence** at the college in five or six years if the depot survives.
feel: Still **anxious**, the same knot I've had since the **takeover** rumours.
S4.quote: A man who might be moving inland doesn't ask anyone out, but a man with ten years might.
fieldNote: For him, AI is a **distant** worry next to the takeover.
Time lets him imagine keeping the **boat** and asking someone out.
His only career step, a **crane licence**, stays years away and depends on the depot.

steps.text: Keep working nights and saving the boat money
Wait for the takeover decision before planning further
Take a crane licence at the college in about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing saved and nowhere in Port Selby to go. What would help is simple: keep the depot here, and if they must cut jobs, give people a year's notice and a proper payout. A year's notice would let a man save something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the night work. Everybody pictures robots in daylight on a nice dry pole. My real job is a gale at three in the morning with the whole street dark. I'd want to see a robot do that before I believe it.

headlineQuote: My real job is a gale at three in the morning with the whole street dark.
portrait: Gareth Mensah, 27, is a **night troubleman** for a coastal power company, working alone.
He has under a month's rent saved and his late father's **fishing boat** to pay for.
A **takeover** that could close his depot worries him more than AI does.
He avoids new tech, leans on his **niece**, and never jumps first.
He is **anxious** throughout and **alarmed** at AGI in two years, with no plan beyond harbour work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with nothing saved and no other work in Port Selby.
whatWouldHelp: If jobs go, a **year's notice** and a proper payout so people can save.
